sections.html:
Fayette County lies in northeastern Iowa. West Union holds the courthouse offices, while Oelwein is the biggest city at 5,920 people in 2020. The 2020 count for the whole county was 19,509, with an estimate of 19,047 for 2025, well under the 29,845 recorded in 1900. Owners occupy 76.1 percent of the 9,298 housing units.

Other sizable towns are West Union (2,490), Sumner (2,030, mostly in Bremer County), Fayette (1,256), Fairbank (1,111), Elgin (685) and Clermont (586). Some sit across county lines. If your mailing address says Sumner or Fairbank, the parcel could belong to another county, so confirm with the parcel record before you hunt for a statement.

With fewer people and older owners, the county sees plenty of inherited and empty houses, and those sellers often face tax, title and condition questions all at once.

West Union is home to both property tax offices: the Assessor decides values and the Treasurer takes payment. Doors are open weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

  • County Treasurer: 114 North Vine Street, PO Box 273, West Union, IA 52175. Phone 563-422-3787. One statement a year, generally mailed during the first week of August.
  • County Assessor: PO Box 167, West Union, IA 52175. Phone 563-422-3397.

Valuations can be searched on the Beacon mapping site. What you owe depends on assessed values and the budgets of schools, cities, the county, townships and community colleges.

sections.h2: Due dates and the assessor's calendar
sections.html:
Pay half by September 30 and half by March 31. Around those two dates, the assessor's calendar looks like this.

Fayette County assessment calendar
DateWhat happens
January 1Assessment date; owners notified by April 1
April 2 to April 25Ask the assessor for an informal review of your value
April 2 to April 30File a written protest with the Board of Review
May 1Board begins meeting and hears appeals through May 31; the Director of Revenue can extend that to July 15
July 1Filing deadline for the homestead credit, disabled veteran homestead credit and military exemption
October 16 to 25Protests of the final equalization order

The assessor revalues real property every second year and expects owners to report new buildings, decks, garages, additions and demolitions. Skipping that report can draw a 100 percent valuation penalty (Iowa Code 441.24). If you built a garage and never told the assessor, deal with it before you list.

sections.h2: Who sits on the Board of Review
sections.html:
The board has three or five people on staggered six-year terms. The Conference Board names them, and it is made up of the Board of Supervisors, the city mayors and one delegate per school district. The roster has to include a farmer, a real estate sales representative and someone from architecture or construction, with no more than two sharing a job.

Use the state form for a written protest, and base it on one of the five grounds in Iowa Code 441.37: unfairness next to similar property, a value over the legal figure, misclassification, a mistake, or fraud. Ask for a hearing when you file. Expect a written ruling that gives reasons.

The homestead credit is giving way to an exemption of 10 percent of taxable value, no lower than $5,500 and no higher than $20,000. Assessment year 2026 is the start, and September 2027 and March 2028 are the first payments to reflect it.

Under the old credit, owners got the tax on $4,850 of value knocked off. Those already enrolled stay enrolled, and the disabled veteran homestead credit continues. Whoever buys your house files for the exemption themselves, and July 1 is the cutoff. If your closing sits close to that date, ask the assessor how the claim is handled.

sections.h2: Selling a house with taxes due
sections.html:
At closing the year's tax is usually prorated, and anything delinquent gets paid first. Because Iowa taxes trail by a year, each bill pays for the fiscal year that ended the prior June 30.

  • A deed signed from July 1 through December 31 leaves the September installment with the seller.
  • A deed signed from January 1 through June 30 leaves the March installment with the seller.
  • Interest of 1.5 percent a month begins October 1 or April 1, never less than one dollar.
  • Transfer tax runs 80 cents per $500 over $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1), and the county recorder receives a declaration of value.

Tax left unpaid can send the parcel to the county sale on the third Monday of June, unless the treasurer picks another day. The treasurer at 563-422-3787 has the current notice list.

Heirs make up a good share of local sellers. Begin at the treasurer's counter for a payoff covering this installment and any older balance. Then ask the assessor whether the parcel has a homestead credit the next owner must replace, and whether a building was added or removed without a report. Armed with that, the title company can settle the tax at the table. Selling to a cash buyer as-is cuts out repair requests, yet the payoff and recording steps are identical.

The assessment calendar and the payment calendar are two separate clocks. The first decides what your parcel is worth, and its deadlines fall in spring, with the equalization protests in October. The second decides when you pay, in September and March. A seller who mixes them up can miss a protest window while worrying about a bill, or the reverse. Write both sets of dates down before you list, and share them with your buyer so nobody is surprised later.

July 1 deserves a circle on the calendar for another reason. It is the filing deadline for the homestead credit, disabled veteran homestead credit and military exemption, so a buyer who closes in June has little time to file.

sections.h2: What to ask the assessor before listing
sections.html: A short phone call to 563-422-3397 can answer several questions at once. Which year was the last revaluation, and when is the next one? Are all buildings, decks and garages on the record? Is a homestead credit attached, and what does a buyer need to do to claim their own? The Beacon site shows the valuation, and printing it for your buyer saves time during negotiation. If you are not sure whether your parcel sits in Fayette County at all, ask the same question about the county line before anything else, because a house near Sumner or Fairbank may belong to Bremer or Buchanan County and be billed there instead. Getting that answer first spares you a wasted trip to the wrong treasurer, and it tells you which assessor to call.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Fayette County, Iowa?
faqs.a: Half by September 30 and half by March 31. Statements usually arrive in early August.

faqs.q: Where do I file a property assessment protest in Fayette County?
faqs.a: Submit it to the county Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. An informal review with the assessor is available from April 2 to April 25.

faqs.q: Does Fayette County revalue homes every year?
faqs.a: No, every second year. The assessment date is January 1 and notices go out by April 1.

faqs.q: Can I sell an inherited house in Fayette County with taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. Money owed is normally paid from proceeds at closing, since delinquent amounts must be cleared for a clean transfer. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure.

faqs.q: Who pays the September or March installment when I sell?
faqs.a: Closing from July 1 through December 31 means you owe September. Closing from January 1 through June 30 means you owe March.
